cue: Hold the phone steady. The world is grey and blurry except where something moves, and a narrow sharp strip of colour turns toward it.

fov.note: the three pairs of side eyes together cover about this much of the circle

cpd.note: a guess in the middle of the 0.3 to 1.3 cycles per degree reported for the front side eyes, which cover most of the field

M.note: the side eyes carry one green receptor class

sat.note: one receptor class gives no colour contrast outside the front strip

gate.note: the side eyes answer to movement only, so still things fade away outside the front strip

glow.note: how brightly movement glows outside the strip

PRINCIPAL.note: ultraviolet and green receptors of the front eyes; the mapping to screen colours is the app's

SIDE.note: the single green receptor class of the side eyes

deg.note: width and height in degrees of one unmoved principal retina

M.note: ultraviolet and green classes of the principal eyes

sat.note: two receptor classes give less colour than a person has

uv.note: the camera records almost no ultraviolet, so blue stands in for it

saccade.note: worked out from a 15 degree turn finished within 0.1 seconds

sweep.note: side-to-side scan across a target, at least 2 degrees across and about a second a cycle

twist.note: the retinae turn about 25 degrees each way, taking about 2 seconds and holding a few seconds

ior.note: a place just inspected is ignored for about 5 seconds

iorDeg.note: a few degrees around the place just looked at

gaze.name: strip
gaze.note: the sharp strip moves over the picture toward what moves

rows: Each of the two big front eyes sees a strip about 2 degrees wide and 21 degrees tall. In Phidippus it resolves about 3.8 cycles per degree, roughly an eighth of what a person reads. Portia reaches 12.5.
Three pairs of smaller side eyes cover about 330 degrees in one jumping spider and almost the whole circle in another. Together they look nearly all the way around the animal.
The front side eyes resolve between 0.3 and 1.3 cycles per degree. Everything outside the front strip is a soft blur, far below a person's sharpness of about 30.

The side eyes behave as though completely blind to stationary objects. A light that only turns on and off sets off no turn, and a small moving thing does. This view fades still things away outside the front strip.

The front eyes carry two kinds of receptor, one for ultraviolet near 360 nanometres and one for green near 530. The side eyes carry a single green kind near 535. This view keeps colour inside the strip and draws the rest in grey.

Behind fixed lenses the front retinas sweep side to side across a target in about a second or two and twist 20 to 30 degrees each way, holding each end for a few seconds. A turn of 15 degrees is finished within a tenth of a second. After the front eyes inspect a spot, the side eyes stop noticing movement there for about five seconds.

The sharpness of the side eyes, the full fade of still things, the glow on moving things, the size of the ignored place, the amount of ultraviolet and the colour level in the strip belong to the app. So do the exact sweep, twist and ignore times, and the mapping from receptor peaks to screen colours. The camera records almost no ultraviolet, so its blue stands in for it, since ultraviolet contrasts in natural scenes most resemble blue ones.
